summary.text: Le Chatelier's principle is used to predict the effect of a change in conditions on chemical equilibrium.
The system opposes the change: adding a species favours the side that counters the addition, and removing one makes the reaction favour the side that lost it.
It can also describe mechanical systems, where a system put under stress responds in a way that reduces that stress.

facts.label: Other names
facts.value: Braun–Le Chatelier principle and the equilibrium law

facts.label: Mechanical example
facts.value: Shear pins protect systems from stress applied in unwanted ways

facts.label: Ester formation
facts.value: Removing water drives the equilibrium process forward

facts.label: Where it can mislead
facts.value: Over-general statements can fail outside thermodynamic equilibrium

items.prompt: In a system that makes methanol, a chemist increases the concentration of CO. What does the principle predict?

options.label: The methanol concentration falls, which lowers the CO further
The methanol concentration stays the same, since only CO changed
The methanol concentration increases, which lowers the total change in CO
The CO concentration rises without limit

items.explain: Increasing the concentration of CO means the principle predicts an increase in the concentration of methanol.

items.prompt: A chemist keeps removing one product from an equilibrium mixture as it forms. What happens to the reaction?

options.label: It favours the side where the product was removed, to fill the gap
It favours the other side, so that the product is used up
It stops, because the mixture can no longer balance
It stays exactly where it was, since removal changes nothing

items.explain: Subtracting a species makes the reaction fill the gap and favour the side where the species was reduced. A product removed continuously can still be obtained.

items.prompt: A chemist wants to push an ester-forming reaction, which also gives off water, towards the ester. What trick helps?

options.label: Add more water so the mixture stays balanced
Cool the mixture so that the water cannot move
Stir it faster so the water stays inside
Remove the water, for example with a desiccant or by distillation

items.explain: Removing water, by desiccants or continuous distillation, shifts condensation equilibria towards the product.

items.prompt: An engineer fits a deliberately weak pin that snaps first under overload, protecting the rest of a machine. Which chemical idea does this echo?

options.label: A catalyst gets used up while speeding up a reaction
A stressed system responds through the mechanism that most easily relieves the stress
A solute stops dissolving once a solution is full
A reaction stops completely when it reaches its barrier

items.explain: A system under stress responds so as to reduce it, generally through the mechanism that most easily relieves it. Shear pins are an engineering application.

items.prompt: Why does adding more of a reactant raise the forward reaction, in terms of collisions?

options.label: Successful collisions of that reactant become more frequent
Each collision becomes much harder
Collisions of the products become rarer
The reactant stops colliding with itself

items.explain: As the concentration of a reactant increases, the frequency of its successful collisions increases, allowing more forward reaction and more product.

items.prompt: A student applies the principle to a system far from thermodynamic equilibrium, and the result contradicts it. What is the likely explanation?

options.label: The principle only works for mechanical systems
The principle only works when no species is added or removed
Over-general statements of the principle can fail outside thermodynamic equilibrium
The principle fails whenever a concentration is changed

items.explain: Outside thermodynamic equilibrium, phenomena can arise that contradict an over-general statement of the principle.
